blocks.text: Wrap an existing class so it satisfies the interface your code expects, without changing either side.

The **adapter** implements the **target** interface your clients use and holds an **adaptee**, usually a legacy class, a vendor SDK or a generated client. It translates calls, data shapes and errors in both directions. The rest of the code never learns the foreign API exists.

items: **Translates:** method names, types, units, error models.
**Contains:** the vendor or legacy coupling in one class.
**Does not:** add behavior; that is Decorator's job.

blocks.text: Prefer an object adapter (composition). A Java class adapter can extend the adaptee and implement the target, but it leaks the adaptee's methods and binds you to one concrete class.

walkthrough.note: The target is the domain's own interface: a typed `Point` and an `Optional` for not found. This is the shape the rest of the code wants.
The adaptee has a different contract: it returns a delimited string and an empty string for failure. You cannot or will not change it.
The adapter implements the target, delegates to the adaptee, and converts both the data (string to `Point`) and the failure signal (empty string to `Optional.empty`).
The client uses `Locator` only. Swapping the legacy service for a new provider means writing another adapter, not editing callers.

blocks.text: Integrating a vendor's payment SDK behind your own port.

The SDK is callback-based, throws its own checked exceptions, and takes amounts in minor units as `long`. Your domain code wants a `PaymentPort` with `Money` and a sealed result type. One `AcmePaymentAdapter` converts amounts, turns callbacks into a return value and maps vendor errors to domain failures. When the vendor changes or a second provider arrives, only that class changes.

lines: interface PaymentPort { PaymentResult charge(Money amount, Card card); }

blocks.text: Payoff: vendor types stop at the adapter boundary, so the domain and its tests never import the SDK.

lists.title: Use when
items: You must use a class whose interface does not match what your code needs.
You want vendor or legacy types confined to one boundary class.
Several providers must be swappable behind one port.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: You own the adaptee; change its interface directly.
The translation is trivial and used once: call it inline.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Leaking adaptee types or exceptions through the target interface.
Mismatched semantics, such as sync versus async or retries, hidden behind one method.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: An adapter between two classes you both own.
A chain of adapters converting back and forth.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: A lambda or method reference is an adapter to any functional interface.
Records make the target's data shape cheap to define.

rows.difference: Decorator keeps the same interface and adds behavior. Adapter changes the interface and adds none.
Facade defines a new, simpler interface over many classes. Adapter conforms one class to an interface that already exists.
Proxy exposes the same interface as its subject and controls access. Adapter exposes a different one.
Adapter reconciles two existing, incompatible interfaces after the fact. Bridge is designed up front so abstraction and implementation vary independently.
Strategy chooses among algorithms built for one interface. Adapter makes a foreign class fit an interface it was not built for.

exercises.scenario: Your domain code expects a `Notifier` interface. A partner library offers `PartnerMailer` with `deliver(Envelope, boolean)`. You cannot modify the library and want the domain to stay independent of it.

options.why: A class that implements `Notifier` and delegates to `PartnerMailer` conforms the foreign API to the expected interface.
A facade would invent a new simplified API over a subsystem; here an existing interface must be satisfied.
Decorator needs both sides to share an interface, and adds behavior; neither is true here.
Bridge is a design-time split into two hierarchies, not a retrofit for an unmodifiable class.

exercises.prompt: Explain Adapter in your own words: what does it change, and how does it differ from Decorator and Facade?

modelAnswer.text: An adapter implements the interface your code expects and delegates to an existing class that has a different one, translating calls, data and errors. It changes the interface and adds no behavior. Decorator keeps the interface and adds behavior; Facade invents a new simpler interface over a subsystem.

keyPoints: Implements the target interface, wraps the adaptee
Translates methods, data shapes and error models
Changes the interface, not the behavior
Decorator keeps the interface; Facade defines a new one
Confines vendor or legacy types to one class
